At an early stage, it’s rarely about pedigree. it’s about whether someone can operate without a map. Structure can be built later. What matters early on is comfort with ambiguity, speed of decision-making, and ownership without constant direction.
I’ve also seen how vague role definitions create silent friction. When expectations aren’t explicit, even strong leaders struggle. Alignment isn’t a soft concept , it’s operational.
Defining the problem before hiring for it makes a huge difference. It forces founders to think clearly about what the business actually needs right now, not what sounds impressive.

Unpopular opinion: Your best engineer would likely fail your technical interview.

Think about the "force multiplier" on your team. The one who:
  • Unfucks the gnarliest production outages at 2 AM.
  • Mentors juniors into senior-level contributors.
  • Navigates 10-year-old legacy code like a mapmaker.

Now, put them in a room. Give them 45 minutes to solve a "Hard" dynamic programming problem on a whiteboard while a stranger breathes down their neck.
❌ They’d probably fail ❌

In decades of software development, I’ve learned that "Interviewing" and "Software Development" have become two entirely different skill sets.

Real development is about pragmatic trade-offs, disciplined testing, and managing complexity. None of that shows up in a LeetCode screen.

If your interview process doesn’t measure what your best people actually do, what exactly are you hiring for?

They hired their first recruiter from Google.
Three months into Series A, hiring had stalled.

She’d hired hundreds of engineers before.

But this was a different game.

At Google, engineers apply.
Thousands of them.

Your job is to filter.

At a 30-person startup nobody has heard of, nobody is applying.

Your job is to create demand.

Two different muscles.

Neither better. Just different.

At Series A, you don’t need pedigree.
You need someone who can build pull from zero.

Someone comfortable reaching out cold.
Someone who can make candidates reconsider their plans.

That rarely shows up on a CV.

And it’s usually the difference between stalled hiring and real momentum.

The number of Recruiters who cannot recruit beyond posting a job is honestly alarming.

Companies are paying agency fees up to 30 percent of a Candidate’s annual salary and in many cases the hiring manager could have found that same person on LinkedIn in about ten minutes.

Posting and praying is not recruiting.

Real recruiting is identifying a market, mapping competitors, engaging passive Candidates, qualifying motivations, and managing both sides of the process from first conversation to acceptance. It is business development, relationship building, and influence. 

Not an Indeed notification.

Large agency training used to create true Recruiters. People who knew how to open doors, run a search, and create value for a client. Somewhere along the way the model shifted to volume activity and software alerts.

If your entire desk stops working when you do not have a job order to post, you do not have a recruiting business. You have a posting habit.

Clients pay fees for access, insight, and control of the hiring process. When you actually recruit, you earn it and everyone wins.

Experienced Recruiters who still believe in building a real desk know exactly what I am talking about.

I reviewed his resume and asked him one simple question:

Are you a finance leader who understands technology?
 Or
Are you a technology leader who understands finance?

There is a difference.

As you climb the leadership ladder, the lines begin to blur.
You’re expected to manage P&L, drive digital transformation, oversee teams, engage stakeholders, optimize processes — everything under one broad umbrella.

And somewhere in that expansion of responsibilities, your core identity starts fading.

You begin to look like “a bit of everything.”
But the market doesn’t hire “everything.”
It hires clarity.

Your resume must make that differentiation unmistakable.

Because if you don’t define your core, 
the market will struggle to position you.
And confusion never converts into callbacks.

Be clear.
Be intentional.
Make recruiters instantly know which role they should call you for.

I’ll be honest — the past few months have been really tough.

I’ve gone through more than 20 interviews. I even traveled onsite for two companies. I filled notebooks with preparation notes, watched hours of lectures, practiced problems late into the night, and barely slept some days trying to prepare well. And still, most of it ended the same way: rejection.

The feedback has been different each time. Sometimes it’s “not enough experience.” Sometimes it’s visa sponsorship limitations. Other times it comes down to missing one hard LeetCode problem after 4–5 interview rounds.

At this point, I’m honestly a bit clueless about what else I could be doing differently. I’m still trying, still learning, and still showing up.

If anyone knows of teams hiring Software Engineers or DevOps engineers, I’d really appreciate being pointed in the right direction.

Most startups don’t fail because of the product.

They fail because of their first leadership hire.

I’ve seen this pattern over and over again.

Founders hire too fast.

They hire on vibes.

They hire someone impressive on paper.

And six months later, everything slows down.

Here’s why the first leadership hire is so hard:

Early-stage companies don’t need “experience.”

They need execution under uncertainty.

Big-company leaders are used to structure.

Startups are mostly ambiguous.

That mismatch quietly kills momentum.

The real issue isn’t talent.

It’s alignment.
Role clarity.
Decision ownership.
Incentives tied to outcomes, not titles.

This is where most founders guess.

And guessing at the leadership layer is expensive.

The 2–4 year engineer isn’t junior.

It’s prime.

And it’s the most competitive hire in engineering and manufacturing right now.

You want someone who:

• Already has real project reps
• Understands production pressure
• Can contribute without hand-holding
• Still has upside
• Isn’t priced like a senior

That’s not entry-level.

That’s premium early-career talent.

And every company is hunting the same profile.

So when you say,
“We just need someone with 2–4 years…”

You’re stepping into one of the most competitive talent battles in the market.

These engineers aren’t hoping.

They’re choosing.

Multiple interviews.
Multiple offers.
Offers accepted before some teams finish debating.

If you’re targeting 2–4 year engineers, you’re not hiring junior talent.

You’re competing for prime talent.

Are you hiring like it?

New from me in The Wall Street Journal: Landing a white-collar job is getting so tough that candidates—not companies—are paying recruiters to match them with positions. That has flipped the traditional recruiting model upside-down. 

Meet the "reverse recruiters": They find positions, customize resumes and even contact current employees. They can charge a set fee or a percentage of an applicant's starting salary once a job is accepted. Or both. But it points to how difficult the current world of online applications is to navigate — and how challenging it is to get a white-collar job right now.

“If you are not paying, you are the product,” said Andre Hamra, Refer’s chief executive. “It incentivizes us to actually help the person.”

At Reverse Recruiting Agency, Alex Shinkarovsky's team charges $1,500 monthly, plus a share of the first year's salary. He has 22 active clients. “Some folks just don’t have time to do it, some folks are scared, some folks are unemployed and on their last effort,” he said.
